system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2143-12-28 18:44:00 to 2144-01-04 18:33:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with sepsis secondary to a chronic right hip wound and suspected osteomyelitis, with additional concerns for urinary tract infection and suprapubic pain. He was transferred from an outside hospital where he had been treated with Unasyn, which was discontinued due to prior resistance and allergies. He started IV daptomycin for Enterococcus infection, to which the organism was sensitive, and oral metronidazole for anaerobic coverage after wound cultures grew Enterococcus and Prevotella. He underwent irrigation and debridement of the right hip with flap grafting and primary closure. Postoperatively, he was maintained on strict bedrest in the left lateral decubitus position with head elevation under 30 degrees. A PICC line was placed for outpatient IV antibiotic administration. His condition stabilized, with controlled pain, stable renal function, and no signs of active UTI. He was discharged to an extended care facility on a 14-day course of daptomycin and metronidazole, with follow-up planned for drain removal and wound monitoring.
problems: Unspecified osteomyelitis, pelvic region and thigh
Late effect of spinal cord injury
Personal history of Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Streptococcus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site, streptococcus, group D [Enterococcus]

HISTORY:  ___ male with chest pain.  Question perforation.

FINDINGS:

Single portable view of the chest.  Left PICC is no longer visualized.  The
patient remains rotated to the left.  The right lung is grossly clear.  There
is dense retrocardiac opacity seen laterally silhouetting the lateral aspect
of the hemidiaphragm.  Osseous structures are again notable for partially
visualized lower thoracic spinal hardware which is not well assessed.  No free
air is seen below the diaphragm on this semi-erect film.  

IMPRESSION:

Left basilar opacity potentially due to atelectasis noting that infection is
not excluded.  Consider repeat PA and lateral if the patient is amenable.

INDICATION:  Fever, tachycardia, and feculent emesis.  Pneumonia on chest
x-ray.  Characterize pneumonia and evaluate for small bowel obstruction.

COMPARISONS:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis from ___.  CT of the
lower extremity from ___.  CT of the right hip from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous axial MDCT images were obtained through the torso
without the administration of IV or oral contrast.  Sagittal and coronal
reformatted images were obtained and reviewed.

FINDINGS:  

CHEST:  The thyroid gland is normal.  There is no axillary, mediastinal, or
hilar lymphadenopathy.  The heart is normal in size.  Trace pericardial fluid
is likely within normal physiologic range.  The main pulmonary artery trunk is
normal in diameter.  The thoracic aorta is normal in course and caliber
without evidence of an aneurysm.  There is very minimal atherosclerotic
disease along its course.

An NG tube is present within the stomach and then curls back into the
esophagus with the tip in the upper esophagus, a few centimeters above the
carina.  The esophagus is distened with a small amount of fluid in the lumen
(2, 25).  Wall thickening is difficult to exclude.  There is a small hiatal
hernia, slightly more prominent than on the prior exam.

The airways are patent to the subsegmental levels.  There are ___
opacities in the left upper and lower lobe with an airspace consolidation
along the posterior left upper lobe and lingula.  Additionally, there is
patchy ground glass opacification in the left lower lobe.  This is most
consistent with infection or aspiration.  There is some volume loss, likely
due to a component of atelectasis.  There is no discrete pulmonary nodule. 
The right lung is clear.  There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

ABDOMEN:  Within the limitations of a non-contrast CT, the liver is normal in
shape and contour without focal lesions.  There is no intra- or extra-hepatic
biliary duct dilation.  The gallbladder, spleen, pancreas and right adrenal
gland are normal.  The left adrenal gland is thickened without a discrete
nodule, similar to the prior exam.  Noted are two accessory spleens.  Again,
the kidneys are atrophic with prominent collecting systems, likely due to
chronic reflux.  Evaluation of the kidneys is difficult due to metallic
artifact from the adjacent spinal fusion hardware, though no definite masses
are identified.  There is no perinephric stranding or fluid collection.

The stomach is normal in caliber.  Some hyperdensity within the body of the
stomach (2, 55) is nonspecific, and could present pooling hemorrhagic fluid. 
Alternatively, it could be food material.  The small bowel is normal in
caliber without evidence of obstruction.  There are no focal inflammatory
changes.  There is no free air or free fluid.  There is no mesenteric,
retroperitoneal, or periportal lymphadenopathy.  The abdominal vasculature is
normal in caliber without significant atherosclerotic calcifications.

PELVIS:  The pelvis is dysmorphic, similar to the prior exam.   A Foley
catheter is malpositioned with the balloon inflated in the distal urethra. 
The tip is in the prostatic portion of the urethra.  The bladder is mostly
collapsed.

There is a large fecal load throughout the colon.  There are no focal
inflammatory changes or evidence of a mass.  The appendix is not definitely
visualized, though there are no secondary signs of appendicitis in the right
lower quadrant.

There is nonspecific stranding along the posterior soft tissues, likely due to
a chronic supine position.  Since the prior CT of the right side of the pelvis
from ___, there has been surgical revision of wound overlying the
right femur.  There is increased soft tissue around the wound.  The amount of
air around the wound has decreased.  There are one or two locules of
subcutaneous air that persist.  There is some nonspecific stranding in the
surrounding soft tissues.  There is a bone fragment adjacent to the greater
trochanter of the femur which has changed in that it no longer appears
continuous with the trochanter where it likely had been on the prior exam. 
This may be related to post-surgical changes.  It is difficult to exclude
infection.  

The last time the left side of the buttock was evaluated by imaging was
___.  Since then, there are no significant changes.  The skin
closely approximates the bone.  There is no definite bone destruction or
erosion to suggest osteomyelitis.  There is no discrete fluid collection.  

There are prominent inguinal and pelvic lymph nodes, though none meet criteria
for pathologic enlargement.  There is no free fluid in the pelvis.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  The patient is status post laminectomies and posterior
fusion from T9 through L2 with pedicle screws at L1 and L2.  The hardware
appears intact and unchanged from the prior exam.  A compression deformity of
T12 has not definitely progressed since the prior exam.  No new fractures are
identified.  Again, the T11/12 disc space is nearly completely obliterated.

The bony pelvis also has a dysmorphic appearance.  There are chronic bilateral
hip effusions, larger on the left than the right, and not significantly
changed from the prior exam.  Superior and posterior dislocation of the left
femoral head with coxa magna/breva and pseudoarthrosis along the left iliac
wing is unchanged.  There is periarticular heterotopic ossification.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital because you came in with fever, abdominal pain, and vomiting that looked like coffee grounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt really bad this morning. The vomiting scared me. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious. You're in septic shock, which means your body is fighting a severe infection. Your blood pressure was low, and your white blood cell count is very high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Septic shock? Like, I could’ve died?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was dangerous, but we’ve started treatment. You have pneumonia in your left lung, which is likely what caused the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did have a cough yesterday. I thought it was just mucus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the CT scan shows infection and some collapse in part of your lung. We’ve started antibiotics—Linezolid and Meropenem—to cover the most likely bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had bad reactions to antibiotics before. I’m allergic to a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Your list is long, but we chose these because they’re safe for you and effective. We also placed a central line in your neck to give meds and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vomiting? Was there bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a concern. You had coffee-ground emesis, which can mean stomach bleeding. Your hemoglobin is low but stable. We gave you two units of blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need another transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll watch it. GI is going to do an endoscopy in a day or two to check your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my kidney numbers? They’re always high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 3.1, which is up from your baseline of 2.4–3.0. But it’s improving with fluids. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are better—white count is coming down, and your oxygen levels are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit less foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching your antibiotics. Your urine grew Pseudomonas, which is resistant to Meropenem. ID recommends cefepime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cefepime? I think I’ve had that before. But I’m not sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Records show you had it without reaction. We’ll start it slowly and watch you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I need to tell you—during the cefepime infusion, you developed a fever, itching, and hives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt it—like something was crawling on my skin. Was it an allergy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, an allergic reaction. We stopped cefepime and gave Benadryl and steroids. You’re okay now, but we’ll avoid that drug in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now for the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching to aztreonam, which is safe for you and covers Pseudomonas. We’re also adding Flagyl for possible anaerobic bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows the pneumonia is starting to clear. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m breathing easier. What about the endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for tomorrow. We’ll look for ulcers or inflammation. In the meantime, we’ve started you on a stronger stomach medicine—omeprazole twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. The EGD was done this morning. You have mild esophagitis and gastritis, but no ulcers or active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not currently. The biopsies were mostly normal. GI says no need for repeat scope. Just stay on the omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also been constipated. Haven’t had a real bowel movement in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed a large stool burden. We’ve started senna and a suppository. You had a small movement yesterday, which is a start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is back to baseline—creatinine is 2.1. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And the antibiotics? How much longer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on day 4 of a 7-day course. We’ll finish the IV antibiotics by discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Plastics checked your right hip wound. It looks healed, no signs of infection. You still need to stay off it—no weight-bearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been lying on my left side like they said. It’s uncomfortable, but I’ll keep doing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard, but it’s important for healing. Also, your urine had some yeast—about 1,000/mL. It’s not a full infection, so no treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my pain meds? I’m still hurting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your home meds—oxycodone IR 60 mg every 8 hours as needed, and the combo pill every 4 hours. PACT is managing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Your white count is normal, you’re off oxygen, and your pneumonia is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, tomorrow. But you need to follow up with your PCP and allergist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Allergist? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of the cefepime reaction. They’ll do skin testing to confirm what you’re truly allergic to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that. And my blood pressure meds—losartan and amlodipine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding them. Your blood pressure is normal without them. You can restart if it goes up, but check with your doctor first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged. Keep taking the omeprazole twice daily, and all your other meds as listed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the wound on my heel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care wanted to see it, but you declined. Keep it clean and protected. See your doctor if it worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest, follow up with your doctors, and call if you feel worse. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with septic shock secondary to bacterial pneumonia and coffee-ground emesis. He was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics, including Linezolid and Meropenem, but developed an allergic reaction to cefepime, which was substituted with aztreonam and metronidazole. An EGD revealed mild esophagitis and gastritis without active bleeding, and he responded well to treatment with omeprazole. His acute kidney injury resolved with hydration, and his constipation improved with a bowel regimen. The right hip wound showed no signs of re-infection, and he remained non-weight-bearing as instructed. He completed a 7-day course of IV antibiotics and was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up planned for allergy testing and primary care.
